Amortization is fine and 180 kernels is a lot, but neither matters if the overhead being removed is tiny. Measure the fraction first.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: You switch from a BERT-based reranker to an XLM-RoBERTa-based one and keep the same max_length. Which detail changes in packing?
options: The query is now placed after the document
There are no special tokens at all
The model accepts 1,024 positions automatically
The pair uses four special tokens and no segment ids, so one fewer document token fits
explain: XLM-RoBERTa packs a pair as <s> A </s></s> B </s> and does not use token type ids. Order and the max_length you pass stay the same; the budget for the document shrinks by one token.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: A colleague proposes caching cross-encoder scores for every (query, document) pair to remove reranking latency. When does this actually help?
options: Only for repeated exact queries (head queries) over an unchanged candidate set; the long tail of new queries still pays full cost
Always, because cross-encoder scores never change
Never, because the scores depend on batch size
Only if the model uses sigmoid outputs
explain: A score is a function of the exact query and document text. Caching works for frequent repeated queries, which Hofstatter et al. also note as the exception, but most queries in real traffic are unique and must be scored live.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Why does a one-time pad not replace AES for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)?
options: Because XOR is too slow on modern CPUs
Because the key must be as long as all the traffic and delivered securely in advance
Because it was broken by quantum computers
Because it cannot encrypt binary data
explain: The pad is unbreakable but its key logistics are impossible at internet scale. Practical ciphers use a short key (16 or 32 bytes) and accept security based on computational difficulty.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Roughly how many random inputs until a collision is likely for a 160-bit hash such as SHA-1, if the hash were ideal?
explain: Birthday bound: about 2^(n/2) = 2^80. Real attacks on SHA-1 do better than that by exploiting its structure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Which Python call should generate a password-reset token?
options: random.getrandbits(128)
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
uuid.uuid1()
hash(time.time())
explain: secrets reads the OS CSPRNG. random is predictable from its state or seed, uuid1 encodes time and the machine address, and hashing the time adds no entropy.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: A teammate proposes encrypting session cookies with AES-CTR and a counter stored in memory that resets to 0 on restart. Which rule does this break?
options: Do not hash passwords
Never reuse a nonce: after a restart the same counter values repeat under the same key, and CTR also lacks authentication
Use constant-time comparison
Retire SHA-1
explain: A counter that resets repeats keystreams (two-time pad), and plain CTR gives no integrity, so cookies could be bit-flipped. Use an AEAD with random or persistent nonces, or a vetted token library.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the shared memory layout is valid for a descriptor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: A client signs a test agreement covering 'all our cloud servers'. One server in the list is actually run by a hosting company on shared hardware. What is the right move?
options: Test it: the client listed it, so it is in scope
Confirm ownership and get the hosting provider's terms or consent before testing anything that is not the client's to authorise
Test it gently, at night, so nobody notices
Skip the agreement and rely on the bug bounty rules of the hosting company
explain: Only someone entitled to control a system can authorise access to it. A client's list proves what the client believes, not what it owns. Many cloud providers publish their own testing policies; read them and keep the result with the agreement.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Under CMA section 5, which fact alone gives a section 1 offence a significant link to England and Wales?
options: The accused speaks English
The target server was in England at the time, even if the accused was abroad
The website uses a .uk domain name
The victim company is listed on the London Stock Exchange
explain: Section 5(2) gives two links for section 1: the accused was in the home country when acting, or the computer containing the targeted program or data was. A domain name or a listing is not on the list.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: A researcher in the US emails exploit details for a router bug to the router vendor's security team abroad, so they can fix it. Which concept in the 2021 BIS rule fits best?
options: Deemed export to an E:1 country
Vulnerability disclosure
Entity List designation
Intrusion software production
explain: The rule defines vulnerability disclosure as identifying, reporting or communicating a vulnerability to people responsible for remediating it, to resolve it. The 2017 Wassenaar change excluded such technology exchanges from the development-technology control.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: Why could Sullivan be convicted of misprision of a felony?
options: Because Uber's bug bounty programme was illegal
Because a security officer must publish every bug
Because the evidence showed the hackers committed a CFAA felony, Sullivan knew it, and took steps to conceal it instead of reporting it
Because the hackers were from another country
explain: The Ninth Circuit explained that misprision needs a completed felony by the principal (here unauthorised access under the CFAA), knowledge of it, and concealment. The NDA could not retroactively authorise the access.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: A colleague's DoReMi port returns the domain weights from the final step instead of the average over steps. What is the likely effect?
options: The output is noisier and reflects only the end of training, while the method (following Nemirovski et al.) returns the average over the trajectory
None, because the weights converge to a fixed point after a few steps
Weights will no longer sum to 1
The proxy model will diverge
explain: Per-step weights react to one minibatch and keep moving as the proxy learns. The paper returns the average over all T steps, which is smoother and integrates the whole run, including the early phase when weights change most.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Your linear regression over 5 domains recommends putting 100 percent of the budget on Wikipedia. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Wikipedia really is the best data and the other domains add nothing
A linear function over mixtures always has its minimum at a corner, so the pick reflects the model's form, not the data
The regression has too many runs and is overfitting
The proxy models were too large
explain: A linear function on the probability simplex is minimized at a vertex, a single-domain mixture. Mixture effects are nonlinear (the first few percent of a domain matter most), which is why RegMix prefers LightGBM and averages the top 100 predicted mixtures.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: Your equivalence test asserts allclose on the logits with atol = 1e-3 and it passes. What has it established about the generated tokens?
options: They must be identical, since the logits agree to within 1e-3.
Very little on its own: a 1e-3 tolerance only protects an argmax whose top-2 margin exceeds 2e-3, and near-ties are far smaller than that.
They are identical as long as the temperature is 0.
Nothing, because allclose is never a valid comparison for logits.
explain: A tolerance d on logits preserves the top-2 ordering only when the gap exceeds 2d. With atol = 1e-3 the test is blind to every position whose margin is under 2e-3, and near-ties can be around 1e-06. A tolerance is usable when it is paired with the margin distribution; the problem is the missing margin check, not allclose itself.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
question: A teammate sets the network drop rate to 50% in every simulation run to "find more bugs". What is the likely effect?
options: More bugs found, since more faults always means more coverage
The cluster rarely makes progress, so the run explores a small, repetitive set of states
Determinism breaks, because drops are random
Nothing, because consensus tolerates any drop rate
explain: The FoundationDB paper explicitly tunes fault distributions to avoid an excessive fault rate that drives the system into a small state space. At 50% loss on every run the cluster mostly retries and times out; deep states such as long recoveries under load are rarely reached. Vary the rate per run instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
question: In the fixed workflow, why does the deploy job also need the production environment, when it already has `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`?
options: The `if:` is cosmetic and GitHub ignores it
Environments make jobs run faster
The `if:` lives in the workflow file, which a branch can edit; the environment's branch rule and reviewers are enforced by GitHub outside the file, and the cloud role can require that environment
Environments are needed to use actions/checkout
explain: A condition written in the workflow is only as trustworthy as the file. A branch can delete it. Environment protection rules are settings the branch cannot change, and an OIDC trust on environment:production means the cloud refuses tokens from any other job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments
question: A job runs on a pull_request event and references the environment `staging`. What subject does GitHub put in its token?
options: repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request
repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/pull/1/merge
repo:ORG/REPO:environment:staging
repo:ORG/REPO
explain: GitHub's reference: the subject includes the environment name when the job references an environment, and includes pull_request only if the job does not reference one.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
question: A developer adds `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_24` with no comment to silence the open-SSH finding. What should the pipeline enforce?
options: Nothing: skips are always fine
Delete all skip comments automatically
Disable CKV_AWS_24 everywhere
Skips must name a reason (and ideally an owner and an end date) and go through review like any exception
explain: Checkov's format includes a suppression comment after the check id. A skip without a reason is an unreviewed exception to policy.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: A self-hosted runner is suspected of running attacker code. What is the right first containment step?
options: Delete suspicious files on it and keep using it
Take it offline and replace it from a clean image, then rotate every secret jobs on it could reach
Restart the runner service
Rename the runner
explain: A persistent runner can hide leftover processes and modified tools (the PyTorch case). Rebuilding from a known-good image is the only state you can trust; secrets that passed through it must be treated as stolen.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
question: Why does DiffuLLaMA keep the 'shift operation' when it turns LLaMA into a diffusion model?
options: Because bidirectional attention cannot work without it
Because the shift makes the KV cache exact
So that the pretrained output at position i keeps predicting the token at i + 1, reusing what the AR weights already learned
Because masked tokens must always be predicted from the right
explain: An AR model's hidden state at i is trained to encode the next token. Keeping that alignment means a masked token is read from its left neighbour's output, so continued training starts close to what the weights already do. Attention is fully bidirectional either way, and caching is unaffected.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
question: An offline batch job summarizes millions of documents overnight. There is no latency SLO; the goal is tokens per dollar. Which design do the sources point toward?
options: Separate prefill and decode clusters on different GPU generations, mandatory for throughput
Colocated serving with chunked prefill to keep every iteration near the compute-bound point
Disaggregation over 25 Gb/s Ethernet to save NVLink
Disaggregation, because it always raises goodput
explain: Goodput only matters when there are SLOs. DistServe's discussion says that in throughput-oriented offline settings, chunked prefill with piggybacking (decode tokens riding along in the batch of each prefill chunk) may be preferred because it fills each batch to the compute-bound threshold. vLLM's docs also note disaggregated prefill does not improve throughput.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
question: Record 812 is marked free and its sequence number is 4. An entry in the NTFS change journal (lesson 6) refers to file reference 812 with sequence 3. What does that tell you?
options: The journal entry describes the same file that the record holds now
The journal is corrupt, because sequence numbers never change
Record 812 is a directory
The journal entry describes an earlier file that used record 812 before it was freed
explain: The sequence number increments each time a record is freed. Sequence 3 in the reference versus 4 in the record means the record has been freed since; the reference points to an older occupant.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: APFS: containers, copy-on-write and snapshots
question: You remove the internal SSD from an Apple silicon Mac with FileVault on and image it with a write-blocker. What do you have?
options: A readable APFS volume, because write-blockers bypass encryption
Encrypted data that stays unreadable without valid credentials or a recovery key
A blank image, because the SSD erases itself
A readable image as long as you image the whole container
explain: Apple documents that internal APFS volumes stay encrypted without valid login credentials or a cryptographic recovery key, even attached to another computer. A write-blocker preserves data; it does not decrypt it.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited
question: The suspect cleared their browser history. What can SRUM still offer?
options: Per-application, per-user network byte counts with timestamps, showing that the browser moved data
The URLs that were visited
The content of the uploaded file
Nothing, because clearing history also clears SRUM
explain: SRUM's Network Usage table records BytesSent and BytesRecvd per application and user. It does not record URLs or content, and the browser's clear-history function does not touch SRUDB.dat.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
question: Which practice most directly addresses the risk that one tool misparses a crucial artefact?
options: Running the same tool twice
Using a newer computer
Hashing the report
Confirming the finding with an independent tool and against the raw data
explain: A second, independent implementation is unlikely to share the first tool's bug, and checking the raw bytes removes tool interpretation. Running the same tool repeats the same error; hashing the report only shows it did not change later.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds
question: In the toy consolidation, why do B's out-neighbors C and F become candidates for p?
options: Because they are p's nearest points
Because RobustPrune always adds every candidate
Because paths that ran p, B, C or p, B, F must be preserved by giving p a chance to link to them directly
Because C and F were on the DeleteList
explain: Algorithm 4 adds the deleted node's out-neighbors to the candidate set of each in-neighbor, so navigation through the hole is preserved. RobustPrune then decides which to keep: here C survives and F is covered by D.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
question: A pair has policy log-probs chosen -30, rejected -20 and reference log-probs chosen -32, rejected -18, with $\beta = 0.1$. What is the DPO margin, and does the implicit reward rank the pair correctly?
options: -1.0, ranked wrong, because the policy gives the chosen answer lower probability
+0.4, ranked correctly, even though the policy still gives the chosen answer lower probability
+1.0, ranked correctly
0, because the reference and policy disagree
explain: Chosen log-ratio: -30 - (-32) = +2. Rejected: -20 - (-18) = -2. Margin 0.1 x (2 - (-2)) = +0.4, so the implicit reward ranks it correctly. Yet the policy itself still prefers the rejected text (-20 beats -30). DPO scores improvement relative to the reference, not raw likelihood; lesson 7 shows why this matters.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
question: A team must align a 7B base model on one GPU with tight memory and has paired preference data but no SFT checkpoint yet. Which method fits best?
options: DPO, because it is the most widely used
KTO, because it needs no pairs
ORPO, because it trains from the base model in one stage with no reference model
IPO, because it regularizes better
explain: ORPO combines the SFT loss with the odds-ratio penalty, so it needs neither a prior SFT stage nor a reference copy of the model. DPO, IPO and KTO all assume a reference (normally an SFT model) is available.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
question: A dual write does `old.increment(counter, 1)` then `new.increment(counter, 1)`, retrying the second call on timeout. After a week the new counters are slightly *higher* than the old ones. What is the most likely cause?
options: Clock skew between the two stores
A timed-out increment had actually been applied, so the retry applied it twice
The backfill copied counters that were already migrated
Last-writer-wins dropped some increments in the old store
explain: A timeout does not mean the write failed. Retrying a non-idempotent delta (add 1) after an ambiguous failure double-applies it. Writing the full current value read from the source of truth, or making the operation idempotent with a request ID, removes the problem.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
question: Why is a kernel module a poor way to add ad hoc tracing to a production machine, compared with an eBPF program?
options: A module cannot read kernel function arguments
Nothing checks the module's code before it runs, so one bad pointer or endless loop can crash or hang the whole machine
Modules can only be loaded at boot time
Modules run in user space and are therefore slow
explain: Modules run arbitrary native code in the kernel with no load-time safety proof. eBPF programs are verified first (termination, initialized registers, in-bounds memory) and only then JIT-compiled and attached.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: Many CPUs increment the same counter. Why does bpftrace recommend @c = count() over @c++?
options: count() uses per-CPU slots, so concurrent updates never collide; @c++ is a non-atomic shared update that can lose increments
@c++ is rejected by the verifier
count() is faster to read than @c++
@c++ sends an event to user space each time
explain: Per-CPU maps make writes cheap and exact. The trade is that reading the value is slower, since every CPU's slot must be summed.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators
question: A team accumulates int8 x int8 products in an int16 register to save space. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, products of 8-bit numbers always fit in 16 bits
Sums overflow: one product can reach about 32,000, so two products can already exceed the int16 maximum
The zero point can no longer be represented
The scale M stops being in (0, 1)
explain: A single product fits in 16 bits, but the dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them. Jacob et al. use an int32 accumulator for exactly this reason. ONNX Runtime documents a related issue with VPMADDUBSW, an x86 vector instruction (AVX2, AVX-512) that adds pairs of 8-bit products into 16 bits and clamps on overflow.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: FortiOS/FortiProxy has 15 KEV entries (12 ransomware-linked); F5 BIG-IP has 8. What can you conclude from these counts alone?
options: BIG-IP is about twice as secure as FortiOS
FortiOS should be banned
Little about code quality: KEV records exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how common and attractive a product is
KEV only covers network products
explain: KEV is evidence of exploitation in the wild, not a defect rate. Deployment size, attacker interest and who investigates all affect the count. Use it to decide what to watch and patch fastest, not to grade vendors on its own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: On 10 January 2024 Ivanti published a mitigation, with patches still weeks away. Which of these did applying the mitigation NOT do?
options: Remove webshells, modified files and stolen passwords from devices already compromised
Block the known route to the vulnerable endpoints
Reduce exposure while waiting for patches
Buy time for a planned rebuild
explain: A mitigation stops new exploitation by the known path. It does nothing about what the attacker already changed or took, which is why Volexity said a mitigation does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Does BOD 23-02 require an agency to take its public VPN portal off the internet?
options: Yes, all VPN services must be internal
No. It covers management interfaces; the VPN service itself may stay public (other rules, such as patch deadlines, still apply to it)
Yes, unless the portal sits behind a separate policy enforcement point
No, because VPN portals count as cloud management interfaces, which are out of scope
explain: The directive defines a networked management interface as one meant exclusively for administrators. The user-facing VPN service is the device's job, so it is not in scope, although BOD 26-04 still sets its patch deadlines.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: Why do Chen et al. measure outcome efficiency instead of just counting tokens?
options: Token counts cannot be compared across tokenizers
Outcome efficiency rewards models for being short even when they are wrong
It separates tokens that led to the first correct answer from tokens spent after it, so a long but necessary trace is not penalized
It is the metric the models were trained on
explain: A 3,000-token AIME solution that is correct only at the end has efficiency near 1. A 900-token answer to 2 + 3 that was right after 39 tokens scores 4.3%. Raw length cannot tell these apart.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
question: Ana's laptop runs signature antivirus only. Word starts PowerShell, which downloads nothing to disk and connects to a remote server. Why might the antivirus stay silent?
options: It judges files one at a time, and no file here matches a known-bad signature; the suspicious part is the sequence of behaviours
Antivirus cannot run on laptops that have Office installed
PowerShell disables antivirus whenever it starts
Antivirus only scans email, never processes
explain: Signature antivirus answers a per-file question. Each file here (winword.exe, powershell.exe) is legitimate. The signal is in the relationships: an Office app starting a shell that then goes online. Recording and correlating those relationships is what EDR adds.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: An admin writes `<ProcessAccess onmatch="include" />` with no rules inside, expecting to see every process access. What does Sysmon log for event 10?
options: Every process access
Only access to lsass.exe
Nothing
Only accesses by unsigned programs
explain: An include filter logs only events that match a rule; with no rules nothing matches, so nothing is logged. To log everything you would use an empty exclude filter (which is usually far too noisy for event 10).

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: A path rule allows `C:\Windows\*`. Why is that weaker than a publisher rule for Microsoft-signed binaries?
options: Path rules are slower to evaluate
Publisher rules also block Microsoft Office
Some folders under `C:\Windows` are writable by ordinary users, so anything a user copies there is allowed; a publisher rule requires the file's signature instead
Path rules only work for DLLs
explain: A path rule trusts a location. Microsoft's default-rules page names `C:\Windows\Temp` as user-writable, so a path rule over the Windows folder lets users run their own files from there. A publisher rule trusts a signature the user cannot forge.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: Which of these would an endpoint sensor on employees' laptops record?
options: A forwarding rule created in cloud webmail from the attacker's own browser
A login to the company VPN appliance
powershell.exe on a laptop opening a handle to lsass.exe
The content of a TLS connection to a web server
explain: Process-to-process handle requests on a monitored host are exactly what sensors record. The webmail rule and VPN login happen on systems with no sensor, and TLS content is encrypted; only metadata such as the destination is visible.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: A 1500 W kettle and a 1500 W space heater (both nearly resistive) live in the same house. Which feature from Hart's pipeline separates them best?
options: Nothing in a single (dP, dQ) step; you need other cues such as typical duration or time of day
Their reactive power steps, since dQ differs
Voltage normalisation, since it rescales each appliance differently
The steady-state tolerance of 35 W
explain: Both are resistive, so dQ is near zero for both and dP matches: the two points land in one cluster. Reactive power only helps when the loads differ in it. Normalisation is applied to the aggregate, not per appliance. Separating them needs extra features such as on-duration or usage patterns, which is why later models add temporal structure.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
question: Your entity graph has a cluster of 40,000 company records that should be about 30 companies. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blocking was too strict
A few false links between large clusters, chained by transitive connected components
The prior lambda was set too low
explain: Strict blocking and a low prior both cause missed links, which make clusters too small. Giant clusters come from false edges: connected components chains them, so one bad edge between two big clusters merges both.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: Which audit activity best catches someone quietly taking over an existing powerful app in your tenant?
options: Update application - Certificates and secrets management (or Add service principal credentials)
Add user
Consent to application
Register device
explain: Taking over an existing app means adding a credential to it, which logs as a certificates and secrets update on the application or added service principal credentials. Consent and new users are other steps of other patterns.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: A tenant blocks device code flow everywhere except for the SharePoint resource. A user's session began with a device code sign-in to SharePoint. They then try to open Exchange Online in the same session. What does Microsoft document?
options: Exchange is blocked, because the session is protocol tracked and the device code policy applies to later requests from it
Exchange is allowed because the user signed in normally
Exchange prompts for a new device code
The policy is ignored for refresh tokens
explain: Microsoft's example is exactly this: protocol tracking keeps the session marked as device code through later refreshes, so a sign-in to Exchange in that session is blocked by the authentication flows policy.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: Why does Microsoft recommend rolling the AZUREADSSOACC Kerberos decryption key at least every 30 days?
options: Because anyone holding a copy of that key can create tickets Entra ID trusts for synced users, so a regular rollover limits how long a stolen copy stays useful
Because Kerberos tickets expire after 30 days
To change the encryption from AES to RC4
Because the key is needed to sync passwords
explain: Entra ID decrypts Seamless SSO tickets with that key, so a stolen copy works like a silver ticket key for the cloud sign-in. Rolling it regularly, and after any AD compromise, retires old copies.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: Why do event loops set O_NONBLOCK on every socket even though they only read sockets the kernel reported as ready?
options: Because epoll refuses to watch blocking sockets
Because nonblocking reads are faster to copy
Because readiness can be spurious, and one blocking read would stall every other client on the loop
Because blocking sockets cannot be written to
explain: epoll watches blocking sockets just fine. But a readiness report is only a hint: the data may have been discarded, or another thread may have consumed it. With a blocking socket that read would put the only loop thread to sleep, and every other connection would wait with it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: The only active timer is due in 250 ms, no idle handles are active and nothing is closing. What timeout does libuv pass to the poll step?
options: 0, so it can check the timer often
-1 (infinite), since timers are handled separately
250 ms: sleep until the nearest timer is due unless I/O arrives first
10 ms, a fixed tick
explain: The libuv rules give 0 only when the loop is stopping, has nothing active, has idle handles, or is closing handles. Otherwise the timeout is the time until the closest timer, and infinity only when there are no timers. The I/O wait and the timer wait are one blocking call.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
question: Why did the 17 null variants in the concrete run look better than the baseline on average?
options: The paired t-test is biased toward the variant
Every comparison reused the same baseline run, which happened to score low on these queries, so the tests are correlated
Holm correction shifts p-values downward
The variants were trained on the test queries
explain: The baseline scored 0.357 while its true quality is 0.402. Every variant was compared to that one unlucky draw, so they all looked better together. Shared baselines make multiple tests correlated, which is why the observed FWER (0.421) differs from the independence formula (0.642).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why attackers then reuse existing code
question: Why did NX alone not end memory-corruption exploits?
options: Because NX can be turned off by any program
Because NX only applies to 32-bit processes
Because NX leaks the canary
Because attackers could still redirect control to code that is already executable, such as functions and instruction sequences in libc
explain: NX blocks running data as code, but a hijacked return or function pointer can target existing executable code. That is the core insight of return-into-libc and of Shacham's return-oriented programming paper.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Protecting returns: shadow stacks and pointer authentication
question: An overflow writes past a buffer using an index, skipping the canary and changing only the saved return address. Which mitigation still catches it at return?
options: A hardware shadow stack, because it compares the return address itself with a protected copy
The stack canary
FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO
explain: The canary is untouched, so its check passes. The shadow stack compares the actual return address with a copy that normal stores cannot change, so any modification is caught.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Turning mitigations on and checking a binary
question: `readelf -lW prog` shows a GNU_RELRO segment, and `readelf -d prog` shows `FLAGS_1 PIE` but no BIND_NOW or NOW flag. What should you conclude?
options: Partial RELRO and PIE: .got.plt is still writable; add -Wl,-z,now
Full RELRO and PIE
No RELRO, because BIND_NOW is missing
Not PIE, because BIND_NOW is missing
explain: GNU_RELRO alone is partial RELRO. Full RELRO also needs immediate binding (BIND_NOW / NOW). PIE is indicated separately by the PIE flag and the DYN file type.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
question: An MoE layer has 16 experts, each the same size as the dense MLP it replaced, with top-2 routing. Compared with the dense MLP, what happens to parameters and per-token FLOPs in that layer?
options: Both grow 16 times
Parameters grow 2 times; FLOPs grow 16 times
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs grow about 2 times, plus a tiny router cost
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs stay exactly the same as dense
explain: Every expert is stored, so parameters scale with N = 16. Each token runs only K = 2 experts, so expert FLOPs are 2 times the dense MLP. The router (one dot product per expert) adds a little on top. With top-1 routing (Switch), expert FLOPs would match the dense MLP.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss
question: An MoE is trained on 64 GPUs, each micro-batch holding 2 sequences, with the balance loss computed per micro-batch. Analysis shows every expert is used about equally on code, math and prose. Which change most directly allows domain specialization?
options: Raise alpha so the balance loss is stronger
Add a router z-loss
Synchronize the expert counts $f_i$ across all micro-batches and compute the balance loss on the global batch
Raise the capacity factor
explain: With 2 sequences per micro-batch, the loss forces each sequence to spread evenly, so code tokens cannot concentrate on code experts. Counting $f_i$ over the global batch only requires the corpus mix to be balanced. A larger alpha tightens the same wrong constraint; the z-loss is about logit size; capacity only changes dropping.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
question: On H100 at $d = 128$, exponentials take about 50% of the matmul time. If FP8 matmuls run at 2x the FP16 rate and MUFU is unchanged, what does that ratio become?
options: 25%, because FP8 values are half the size
50%, unchanged
About 100%
About 200%
explain: $T_{exp}/T_{MMA} = r_{MMA}/(4 d\, r_{exp})$. Doubling $r_{MMA}$ doubles the ratio from 0.5 to 1.0: the exponentials now take as long as the matmuls. The FlashAttention-3 paper says exactly this: "the matmul throughput doubles but the exponential throughput stays the same."

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
question: What is the main reason FlashAttention-4 uses the 2-CTA MMA mode in the backward pass?
options: To double the tensor core FLOPs available to each CTA
To cut shared memory traffic (each CTA stages half of operand B) and halve dQ atomic adds
To make the backward pass deterministic
To fit five accumulators in tensor memory
explain: The backward pass is limited by shared memory bandwidth (3328 vs 2560 cycles). Pairing CTAs means each stages half of B, and the dS exchange lets each CTA own half of the dQ tile, halving atomics. Peak FLOPs are unchanged, and determinism comes from the separate semaphore mode.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
question: Doubling Euler steps from 8 to 16 on the toy cut the endpoint error from about 0.135 to about 0.067. What does that ratio indicate?
options: Error is roughly proportional to step size, so Euler is first order
Euler is a second-order method
The flow is straight
The network is overfitting
explain: Halving h roughly halved the error, which is first-order behavior: global error proportional to h. A second-order method like Heun would cut it by about 4x.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
question: You fix the race by making the increment one atomic step (and remove tmp from the spec): `Inc(p) == pc[p] = "inc" /\ x' = x + 1 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "done"]`. What does TLC report for N = 2?
options: Still a violation, because two processes can run Inc in the same step
No error: every step increments x by 1, so x = 2 once both are done
A deadlock error, because Inc can never be enabled
It cannot check it, since x' = x + 1 is an assignment
explain: Next allows exactly one process to take one step at a time, so nothing interleaves inside Inc. TLC confirms it: 4 distinct states, no error (8 states for N = 3). In PlusCal the fix is to put the read and write under one label.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
question: In TwoPhase, the TM receives a Prepared message, which changes only tmPrepared. What does TCommit see under the refinement mapping?
options: A Prepare step by that RM
A stuttering step, because rmState is unchanged
A violation, since TCommit has no TM
Nothing: refinement checking skips steps that change hidden variables
explain: The mapping exposes only rmState. A step that leaves rmState unchanged maps to a stuttering step, which every TLA+ spec allows. TLC does not skip it; it checks that it is a stutter.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
question: A small Rust function parses a length-prefixed packet using unsafe pointer arithmetic, with inputs up to 64 bytes. You want a counterexample if any input can cause out-of-bounds access, with minimal annotation. Which fits best?
options: TLA+ with TLC
P
TLAPS
Kani with a harness over any 64-byte input
explain: This is a code-level, bounded question about one function: exactly what Kani's harnesses and kani::any() are for, and Kani checks for undefined behavior in unsafe code. TLA+, P and TLAPS work on design models, not on the Rust code.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: A team turns on FP8 GEMMs for every linear layer and expects peak memory to halve. It barely changes. Why?
options: FP8 tensors are padded to 16 bits in memory
Most memory is master weights, gradients, optimizer moments and activations that FP8 GEMM inputs do not touch
The amax history uses more memory than the weights
Tensor cores cannot read FP8 from memory
explain: FP8 GEMMs change compute, not the 12 to 16 bytes per parameter of training state. FP8-LM cut memory by moving the gradient and first moment to FP8 and the master weight and second moment to FP16, and DeepSeek-V3 caches activations in FP8.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: Why does the recipe use 16x16 2D blocks for weights but 1x16 blocks for activations and gradients?
options: 2D blocks are faster for every tensor
Activations cannot be transposed
1x16 blocks are required by E4M3
Weights are reused in both Fprop and Dgrad (transposed), so a scale shared over a square block keeps the two quantized copies identical; activations and gradients benefit more from finer 1x16 scaling
explain: The chain-rule mismatch matters most for weights, and weights can adapt to coarser scaling during training. The report found training less sensitive to inconsistency in activations, so they keep the more accurate 1x16 blocks.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
question: A server has a single active client and commit_delay = 2000 microseconds with commit_siblings = 0. What happens to that client?
options: Each commit gets about 2 ms slower and throughput drops, since nobody else can join
Nothing, since commit_delay is ignored with one client
Commits get faster because flushes are batched
Commits become asynchronous
explain: With commit_siblings = 0 the sibling check always passes, so the lone leader sleeps 2 ms before every flush with no one to share it. That is pure added latency. The default commit_siblings = 5 exists to skip the sleep when joiners are unlikely.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Coverage-guided fuzzing: how AFL's edge bitmap steers mutation
question: What does the shift in prev_location = cur_location >> 1 achieve?
options: It makes A then B land in a different slot from B then A, and keeps a block jumping to itself distinct
It halves the map size
It randomises block numbers at run time
It counts how many times each block ran
explain: Without the shift, A XOR B equals B XOR A, and A XOR A is zero for every block, so direction and tight loops would be lost. Shifting the previous location breaks that symmetry.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
question: What does libFuzzer's -merge=1 MIN corpus/ do?
options: Copies into MIN only the inputs from corpus/ that add coverage not already in MIN
Deletes crashing inputs from corpus/
Merges two fuzzers into one process
Minimises each input to its smallest size
explain: The docs: inputs from the second and later directories that trigger new coverage are merged into the first. It shrinks a corpus to a coverage-equivalent subset; per-input shrinking is a different feature (-minimize_crash or reduce_inputs).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing beyond C: Go, Rust, Python and property-based testing
question: What is the oracle in the Hypothesis example?
options: The property decode(encode(name)) == name, which must hold for every generated string
A crash or hang
AddressSanitizer
Code coverage
explain: Property-based testing finds wrong answers, not just crashes. The round-trip property caught a failure that raises nothing at all: the two-character string U+0080 then "0" decodes back as U+0080 alone, a silently wrong answer. The cause is that the length byte counts characters instead of bytes.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
question: Why did OSS-Fuzz's long-running SQLite fuzzing miss the bug Big Sleep found?
options: The OSS-Fuzz harness was not built with the generate_series extension, and AFL on the right binary did not find it in 150 CPU-hours
SQLite has no fuzz targets
The bug only occurs on Windows
Fuzzers cannot find stack bugs
explain: The Big Sleep post: the harness configuration left the extension out, and a dedicated AFL attempt with the needed keywords still failed. Reach and difficulty, not lack of fuzzing, explain the miss.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
question: You are building a structure whose correctness depends on the triangle inequality (lesson 5). Which distance is unsafe to plug in?
options: Levenshtein
Indel
Optimal string alignment (OSA)
True Damerau-Levenshtein
explain: OSA violates the triangle inequality: CA to AC is 1, AC to ABC is 1, but CA to ABC is 3. A search structure that prunes with that inequality could skip a real match. Levenshtein, Indel and true Damerau-Levenshtein are metrics.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
question: A plate solver's answer is described by pointing, rotation and field of view. How many continuous numbers is that?
explain: Pointing on the sky is 2 numbers (RA and Dec), plus 1 rotation angle, plus 1 scale. Lang et al. describe the hypothesis space as continuous and four-dimensional, which is why exhaustive search is impractical.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
question: During verification, star 3 of a true alignment is a satellite with no catalog counterpart. Why does the foreground model include a distractor term d instead of putting all probability on the predicted catalog stars?
options: Without it, any single unmatched star would give a ratio near zero and could veto a correct alignment
To make the computation faster
Because the background model also has a distractor term
To make the false positive rate exactly zero
explain: If F gave zero probability to stars away from predictions, one artifact, planet or catalog gap would multiply K by almost zero. The mixture with d = 0.25 caps the penalty at about -0.6 in log10 per stray star, so real images with junk still solve.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
question: Near the Louvre, 7-character geohash cells are about 153 m tall and 100.5 m wide. Which precision should a 100 m radius query use with a 3 x 3 covering?
options: Length 6, because longer geohashes are always slower
Length 7, the longest whose cells are at least 100 m on both sides here
Length 8, because smaller cells mean fewer false positives
Any length works, since 9 cells always cover the circle
explain: Length 7 cells are just over 100 m in both directions, so the 3 x 3 block is guaranteed to cover the circle with the least overfetch. Length 8 cells (about 19 to 38 m) are smaller than the radius, so 9 of them miss matches. Length 6 is correct but reads many more candidates.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
question: You resize a 4-pixel row to 2 pixels with nearest neighbour. Which source indices does the half-pixel convention read, and which does the floor convention read?
options: Both read 0 and 2, because floor of a half-integer rounds down
Half-pixel reads 1 and 3; floor reads 0 and 2
Half-pixel reads 0 and 2; floor reads 1 and 3
Both read 1 and 3, because the half is added before scaling
explain: Half-pixel: floor((0 + 0.5) x 2) = 1 and floor((1 + 0.5) x 2) = 3. Floor convention: 0 x 2 = 0 and 1 x 2 = 2. At this scale the two conventions never agree on a single pixel, and the half-pixel one reads the source pixel that covers the output pixel's center.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
question: A pipeline resizes 64 crops of 256x256 one at a time, synchronizing after each to check for errors. Measurements show the GPU busy about 6 percent of the time. What is the single best change?
options: Switch the interpolation from bilinear to nearest to halve the arithmetic
Increase the block size so each kernel has more parallelism
Use pinned host memory for the output buffers
Batch all 64 crops into one launch and synchronize once at the end
explain: At 0.44 microseconds of kernel work against 6.7 microseconds of exposed launch overhead, utilization near 6 percent is exactly what the model predicts. Removing 63 launches and 63 synchronizations is the only change that attacks the dominant term. Interpolation arithmetic and block size are irrelevant when the kernel is not the bottleneck, and pinned memory addresses host transfers, not launch overhead.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
question: Which workload benefits most from expandable_segments?
options: Batched inference where the batch size changes slightly between iterations
A model whose tensor shapes are identical every iteration
A job that only allocates 1 KiB tensors
A program that shares every CUDA tensor with worker processes via IPC
explain: Fixed segments work well when sizes repeat exactly. Drifting batch sizes create slightly larger tensors that leave slivers in old segments. Small-only workloads already pack into 2 MiB segments, and IPC sharing is not supported for expandable memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
question: A kernel reads `x[i * 4]` (floats) for consecutive `i` across a warp, and each element is used once. What fraction of fetched bytes is useful, ignoring cache reuse?
explain: Threads are 16 bytes apart, so each 32-byte sector holds 2 requested floats: 16 sectors per warp for 128 useful bytes. 128 / (16 x 32) = 25%.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Reading the Speed Of Light rows
question: Why does Nsight Compute define Memory Throughput as the maximum over its constituent counters instead of their sum?
options: Because summing could exceed 100 percent and look wrong
Because L1, L2 and DRAM counters are collected in different replay passes and cannot be added
Because a throughput is meant to say how close some unit got to its own peak, and the binding constraint is the unit nearest its own ceiling
Because DRAM always dominates the other memory units
explain: The metrics guide defines a throughput as how close a portion of the GPU came to peak rate, and says throughput metrics return the maximum percentage of their constituents, chosen to represent the parts of the pipeline that govern peak performance. The slowest relative unit is what limits you, so the max is the meaningful aggregate; the breakdown then names which unit it was.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
question: A, B and C are allocated with cudaMallocManaged (unified memory, readable by host and device). The host launches `vecAdd<<<4, 256>>>(A, B, C)` and on the very next line prints `C[0]`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: a kernel launch blocks until the kernel finishes
The launch is asynchronous, so the host may read C before the kernel has written it; call cudaDeviceSynchronize() first
Only block 0 has finished by then, but C[0] belongs to block 0 so it is fine
Unified memory cannot be read by the host after a launch
explain: The guide states that kernel launches are asynchronous with respect to the host thread: the kernel may not have finished, or even started. Its unified memory example calls cudaDeviceSynchronize() before the host touches the results. Blocks also have no guaranteed order, so 'block 0 finishes first' is not a safe assumption either.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
question: You port a CUDA kernel to Metal and dispatch it with `dispatchThreads` for exactly N threads. The CUDA version had `if (i >= N) return;` at the top. What should you do with that check?
options: Keep it: Metal always rounds the grid up to whole threadgroups
It becomes redundant: with nonuniform threadgroups Metal launches exactly N threads, though keeping it is harmless
Replace it with threadgroup_barrier, which skips out-of-range threads
Change it to `if (i >= N * threadExecutionWidth)`
explain: dispatchThreads takes the total thread count and creates smaller edge threadgroups, so no thread position exceeds the data. Apple notes you do not need the position check in that case. With dispatchThreadgroups you would need it, just as in CUDA.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
question: In the map step, one batch returns only points with importance score 0. What happens to them?
options: They are filtered out before the reduce step
They are kept but sorted last
They trigger a retry with a larger batch
They are replaced by raw text chunks
explain: Both the paper and the repo drop score-0 answers. If every map answer scores 0, the repo returns a canned "I do not know" unless general knowledge is explicitly allowed.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
question: A team's math verifier compares strings after stripping whitespace. Training stalls on problems whose labels are fractions like 1/2. What is the most likely bug?
options: The KL coefficient is too small
The group size is too large
The policy writes equivalent forms such as 0.5 that the verifier scores 0, so correct reasoning is never rewarded
The verifier gives reward to wrong answers
explain: String matching treats 0.5 and 1/2 as different. Correct solutions get reward 0, so the policy receives no signal on exactly those problems. Normalizing answers (or checking mathematical equivalence) fixes it.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
question: Why did DeepSeek-R1-Zero use rule-based rewards instead of a neural reward model for reasoning tasks?
options: They observed neural reward models being reward-hacked during large-scale RL, and retraining them adds cost and complexity
Neural reward models cannot read long chains of thought
GRPO is mathematically incompatible with learned rewards
Rule-based rewards produce longer responses
explain: That is the stated rationale in the paper. GRPO itself works fine with learned rewards (DeepSeekMath used one), and R1's final stage does use preference reward models, briefly.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
question: Your app needs the scheduled arrival time of trip T1 at stop S3. Which tables must you read?
options: routes.txt and stops.txt
trips.txt and calendar.txt
stop_times.txt, filtered by trip_id = T1 and stop_id or stop_sequence
frequencies.txt, because every trip has a headway
explain: Times live only in stop_times.txt, one row per (trip_id, stop_sequence). trips.txt names the route and service but has no times. frequencies.txt is optional and only used for headway-based or compressed trips.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
question: Your poller sees header timestamps 08:10:30, then 08:10:00, then 08:11:00 from a feed behind a load balancer. What should it do with the 08:10:00 message?
options: Apply it, because the newest download always wins
Merge it with the 08:10:30 message entity by entity
Ignore it and keep the 08:10:30 state, since the timestamp went backwards
Stop polling, the feed is broken
explain: Best practices say the header timestamp should not decrease, and describe exactly this load balancer case. Keeping the newest state by timestamp avoids flicker between replicas.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
question: You sample cycles with `perf record -c 3000000` on a core running steadily at 3 GHz. The program uses 2 seconds of CPU time. About how many samples do you get?
explain: 2 s x 3 GHz = 6 billion cycles; one sample every 3 million cycles gives 2000 samples. The 4000 Hz default only applies with frequency mode, not with -c.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Constant-time comparison in C, measured on a real machine
question: Which change turns leaky_equal into a constant-time function without other changes?
options: Compile with -O3 so the loop runs faster
Replace the loop body with diff |= a[i] ^ b[i] and return diff == 0 after the loop
Add a random usleep() before returning
Compare from the last byte to the first instead
explain: Accumulating differences and deciding once after the loop removes the data-dependent early exit. Speed, reversed order and random sleeps all keep the dependency.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Spectre variant 2: injecting indirect branch targets
question: What does a retpoline rely on to prevent branch target injection?
options: It encrypts function pointers
It turns the indirect jump into a return whose prediction comes from the RSB entry it created itself, so the BTB is never consulted
It disables the branch predictor completely
It moves the branch target into the kernel
explain: The direct call plants a known RSB entry that leads to a harmless loop; the real target is taken from the stack only when the return resolves. Attacker training of the BTB is never used.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Rowhammer: flipping bits in memory you never wrote
question: A vendor says its DDR4 modules are 'Rowhammer-free because of TRR'. Which finding best tests that claim?
options: Kim et al. 2014 on DDR3
The Project Zero NaCl exploit
Cold boot attacks
TRRespass 2020, which flipped bits on 12 of 42 DDR4 modules by hammering many rows at once
explain: TRR tracks a limited number of aggressor rows. Many-sided hammering overwhelms the tracker, which TRRespass demonstrated on DDR4 modules sold with TRR.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
question: A service builds a 4 GiB in-memory index at startup, then serves random lookups for weeks. Which benefit of backing the index with 2 MiB pages stops mattering after warm-up?
options: Each TLB entry covering 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB
Page walks of three levels instead of four
Smaller page tables that stay cached more easily
Taking one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512
explain: Page faults happen only on first touch of each page, so after warm-up there are none to save. Reach, walk length and page-table size affect every lookup for the lifetime of the mapping, which is why the kernel docs call them the important factors.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
question: /proc/vmstat shows thp_fault_fallback growing almost as fast as thp_fault_alloc on a host that has run for months, with defrag set to never. What does this most directly indicate?
options: Faults often find no free 2 MiB block and fall back to 4 KiB pages
The application calls munmap on partial huge pages
The hugetlb pool is exhausted
khugepaged is splitting pages
explain: thp_fault_fallback counts faults that could not allocate a huge page or charge it to the process's memory control group (count it against that group's limit) and used small pages instead. With defrag=never the kernel never compacts at fault time, so a fragmented long-running host falls back often. Partial munmap shows up as thp_split_pmd, and the hugetlb pool is a separate mechanism.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Jamba-v0.1's config has 32 layers, attn_layer_period 8 and attn_layer_offset 4. Which layers (0-based) are attention?
explain: Attention sits where layer index mod 8 equals 4: layers 4, 12, 20 and 28. The other 28 layers are Mamba, giving the 1:7 ratio.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
question: Your hybrid is fine on single-document QA but drops on multi-document QA built by packing unrelated passages. What is the most plausible cause based on the NVIDIA study?
options: The attention layers lack RoPE
The SSM layers' state gets confused by irrelevant documents, possibly from training on packed unrelated sequences
The KV cache is too large
The MLP ratio is too high
explain: Waleffe et al. hypothesized that SSM states are confused by documents irrelevant to the question, and that their long-context recipe of packing unrelated sequences may teach the SSM layers to treat separate documents as related.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
question: Why not run the cross-encoder over the whole corpus instead of retrieving first?
options: Cross-encoders only accept documents found by BM25
Cross-encoders are less accurate than BM25 on long lists
It would require normalizing scores first
It needs one full transformer pass per (query, document) pair at query time, and nothing can be precomputed per document
explain: Because query and document are encoded jointly, there is no document vector to index ahead of time. Cost scales with the number of candidates, which is why it is used as a second stage over tens to hundreds of documents.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: What HyDE achieves, and how query2doc differs
question: On TREC DL19, HyDE has lower nDCG@10 than ANCE (61.3 vs 64.5) but higher recall@1k (88.0 vs 75.5). What is the most reasonable reading?
options: HyDE is broken on precision
HyDE finds more of the relevant documents somewhere in the top 1000, while ANCE orders its top 10 better; a reranker on HyDE's candidates could exploit that
Recall@1k is meaningless for web search
ANCE uses more labels, so its recall should be higher
explain: The paper notes ANCE's better nDCG@10 but lower recall, suggesting bias toward a subset of queries or documents. High recall makes HyDE a good first-stage candidate generator; precision at the top can come from a reranker.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
question: In the ladder, why does the pump keep running when the level is at 250 cm after starting at 195?
options: Because the PUMP contact in the parallel branch (seal-in) keeps rung 3 energised until HIGH or ESTOP breaks it
Because LOW is still true at 250
Because the HMI is holding the pump on
Because outputs are only written once a minute
explain: LOW is false at 250. The seal-in branch uses the pump's own state to stay on, which is how two-setpoint (hysteresis) control avoids switching the pump on and off rapidly around one value.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
question: An OPC UA server supports SignAndEncrypt but also exposes an endpoint in mode None. What is the risk?
options: None: clients always pick the strongest mode
A client or attacker can connect without signatures or encryption, bypassing the protections
Mode None encrypts but does not sign
It only affects performance
explain: Security modes are chosen per connection. Leaving None enabled leaves an unprotected door; the specification says the None profile is for testing and should be disabled by default when secure profiles are available.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Triton and the attack on a safety system
question: Which single change would have most directly prevented the program change on the Triconex controllers?
options: Faster internet at the plant
Keeping the controllers' key switch in RUN except during approved programming
A bigger historian
Disabling the HMI screensaver
explain: With the key in RUN the controller refuses program changes from the network, whatever the attacker controls upstream. Mandiant made this its second recommendation.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
question: Why must the 'golden' PLC logic backup be kept offline?
options: Offline storage is faster
An attacker who altered the PLC may also alter or hide changes in online copies and tools, so the reference must be out of reach
PLCs cannot read online backups
Regulators forbid online backups
explain: Stuxnet hid its blocks from the engineering software. A reference copy that the attacker cannot reach, compared using a clean machine, is the only trustworthy baseline.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SAML web SSO step by step: AuthnRequest, bindings and RelayState
question: Why does the SP put a fresh ID in its AuthnRequest and expect it back as InResponseTo?
options: To choose which signing key the IdP uses
To compress the request
Because the Redirect binding requires a numeric ID
To tie the response to a login this browser actually started, blocking unsolicited and injected responses
